We argue a spectral direction is a candidate causal object only after passing an explicit identification stage (prospective detection, external separation, projector stability, and a quantitative feature-specificity gate), and that whether it is manipulable then depends on the operator in which curvature is measured. Our central finding is a clean dissociation: the causal object exists but lives in different spaces for different problems. In an analytic teacher-student model, prospectively suppressing the detected full-Hessian outlier slows feature-alignment growth by $63.5%$ versus a $26.3%$ norm-matched-random floor ($30$ seeds, $p<10^{-5}$), with a monotone dose-response, an energy-matched control isolating direction from removed update amount ($\approx 0%$ effect), a positive-curvature-branch localization, and a theory-predicted $p{=}1$/$p{=}2$ dissociation with placebo interactions equivalent to null.
